assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, combine many atoms with Lamb-Dicke confinement and now reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. This is a new way of measuring time, which fits the view that progress is limited by what can be measured and how precisely. It enables relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and a redefinition of the second. The idea is clear and original, and it has been demonstrated carefully many times.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and made the first Sr demonstrations. Ye's group drove the accuracy and stability records, which depended on laser stabilization and frequency-comb work. Two names give a fair, compact configuration. The honest question is how to treat Ye's wider precision-measurement and comb context and the single-ion clock work, which was already recognized (Wineland 2012, Hall and Hänsch 2005).
assessment.maturity: Many independent labs (NIST, PTB, SYRTE, RIKEN, JILA, NPL and others) confirm it, with inter-laboratory comparisons and operation outside the lab. The timing is good. The remaining step is the formal redefinition of the second, which is not required for a prize.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wants the clock as an instrument or sees it as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Exact division of credit between the lattice concept and the later accuracy demonstrations is judgment, not independently verified by me.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light for interferometry beats the shot-noise limit in a real instrument. Caves's 1981 analysis showed it was possible. Squeezing experiments followed, and squeezed vacuum is now routinely used in the gravitational-wave detectors, which makes the impact concrete and measurable. This is a standard measurement case: a quantum resource improves the sensitivity of the most precise instruments we have.
assessment.attribution: Caves is the clear theoretical origin. Kimble's group made the first squeezed-light generation (1985-86) and its relevance to metrology. Schnabel did the GEO600 and LIGO-relevant engineering with frequency-dependent squeezing. Mavalvala and others (Slusher, Walls, Vahlbruch, McKenzie) are credible alternatives. Three names is a defensible but contestable set, so the allocation is not settled.
assessment.maturity: Squeezing is used in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600 with clear observed gains in sensitivity, so confirmation is strong. The technique is stable and mature, and the timing is good given that the detectors are already the object of a prize.
uncertainties: Several equally strong contributors are left out of any three-person set.
Part of the credit goes to LIGO engineering teams, not only to quantum-optics groups.
I did not independently check the exact dB gains reported.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry turns matter-wave coherence into a precision sensor: gravimetry, gradiometry, measurement of the fine-structure constant and tests of equivalence principle. The first demonstrations (1991) opened an instrument class that others now use. The scientific idea is original and well tested in the lab, and field-deployed devices are appearing. Applications such as gravimetry resemble what I would expect from quantum sensors.
assessment.attribution: Early work was done in parallel: Mlynek's group (double slit with atoms), Pritchard (MIT, nanofabricated gratings), Kasevich and Chu (Raman light-pulse interferometer) and Chu already got the 1997 prize for cooling. Kasevich-Chu is the decisive step for precision sensors, so leaving out Chu's group could be seen as a problem. The credit is plausible but not obviously clean.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmation is extensive (Stanford, Paris, Hannover, Birmingham, ANU and others), and precision numbers are reproducible. Field-ready devices are still developing, so real-world impact is not yet fully proven.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 1997 and 2001 prizes on cooling and condensates complicates the credit.
Fair attribution among Pritchard, Kasevich and Mlynek versus Chu and others is uncertain.
Technological impact beyond the lab is still emerging.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Spherical-aberration correction brought electron microscopy to sub-angstrom resolution, an instrumental advance that changed how matter is observed at atomic scale in physics and materials. It is a new measurement capability with a large impact on other fields, which I weigh heavily. The underlying idea (Scherzer's theorem could be circumvented with multipole correctors) was a clear, original optical design.
assessment.attribution: Rose designed the corrector theory, Haider and Urban built and demonstrated the working system (with Uli Dahmen, Krivanek and others in related efforts). The three names correspond to the known theory-plus-realization split, which makes this a clean configuration. Krivanek (STEM correctors) is the strongest missing name.
assessment.maturity: Correctors are widely deployed and the resolution gain is reproducible and verified. Recognition is already supported by the Wolf and Kavli prizes. The question is whether a physics prize prefers the instrument over a physics discovery, given the 1986 prize for the electron microscope.
uncertainties: Krivanek's role in STEM aberration correction may need to be recognized, which would break the three-person limit.
Possible view that this is a materials or chemistry instrument rather than physics.
Precedent from the 1986 prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Single NV centres in diamond give optically read-out spins with long room-temperature coherence, which supports nanoscale magnetometry, thermometry and biological sensing. It is a case where a solid-state quantum system becomes a measurement tool with wide applications. The first single-spin optical detection (1997) and later coherent control are experimental landmarks.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup (1997 single-spin ODMR) and Jelezko (coherent control, nuclear-spin registers) are the clear experimental originators. Lukin and the Harvard group developed nanoscale magnetometry and the quantum-network use. Others (Awschalom, Hanson, Walsworth, Budker, Yacoby) also have strong claims, so the three-name set is open to dispute.
assessment.maturity: Many groups confirm it, and commercial NV sensors and diamond-based quantum-network nodes exist. Some of the headline applications (in-vivo sensing, NMR at nanoscale) are still maturing, so timing could be a bit early for the sensing impact.
uncertainties: Credit is spread over many groups, with no obvious single three-person set.
Impact in biology is not yet routine.
The relative importance of the sensing versus the quantum-network use is not settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Light-matter quantum interfaces underpin quantum memories, repeaters and networks. The Cirac-Zoller-Kimble-Mabuchi proposal (1997) set out how to move quantum states between flying photons and stationary atoms, and was followed by atomic-ensemble and single-atom demonstrations. From my own work on rare-earth crystals I know this is hard in practice, with efficiency, storage time and fidelity as limiting numbers. The concept is important and the experiments are real but still short of a deployed technology.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are the central theorists, and Kimble contributed both theory and the early cavity-QED experiments. This is a reasonable trio, but it overlaps strongly with other quantum-information candidates, and ensemble-memory pioneers (Lukin, Polzik, Lvovsky, Gisin, and the solid-state memory groups) may be left out.
assessment.maturity: Experimental progress is steady, with multi-node demonstrations (Hanson, Lukin, Rempe, Pan) but no routine network. The field is still active, so I think it is slightly early.
uncertainties: Overlap with the other Cirac and Zoller candidates.
Attribution split between proposal and experiments is unclear.
Practical quantum-network performance is not yet established.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made strong coupling between a superconducting qubit and a microwave resonator controllable and readable, and became the architecture for most superconducting quantum processors. The measurement-based approach (dispersive readout) is of particular interest. Experiments by Wallraff (2004) and later by Schoelkopf's group are experimental landmarks, and the theory by Blais et al. gave the framework.
assessment.attribution: Blais-Huang-Wallraff-Girvin-Schoelkopf (2004) is the founding paper, with Girvin as a notable absentee from the trio. Credit is clear in structure, but the list leaves out Girvin and others. The 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits (Clarke, Devoret, Martinis) reduces the room for another circuit prize soon.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed and reproduced widely. Practical impact is high, but the quantum-computing outcomes are still uncertain, and a further superconducting-circuit prize so soon after 2025 may be premature.
uncertainties: Girvin's role and the exact set of laureates are open.
Overlap with the recent 2025 superconducting-circuit prize.
Whether the committee views this as engineering of a platform rather than a discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade gives controllable, strong atom-atom interaction, and optical-tweezer arrays have become a programmable platform for quantum simulation and computing. Experimental demonstrations of blockade and of arrays of tens to hundreds of atoms are impressive, and the control and readout (fluorescence imaging) are measurement achievements in their own right.
assessment.attribution: The Jaksch-Cirac-Zoller-Lukin proposals gave the blockade theory (2000-2001), while Saffman, Browaeys and Lukin did decisive experiments. Gaetan, Urban and Grangier showed blockade experimentally, and Bernien and Endres (2017) the programmable arrays. This is a complicated credit set, so a fair trio is not obvious.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly developing, with strong independent confirmation, but the field is still young. Quantum advantage over classical computing has not been established, so I think this is premature compared with the candidates above.
uncertainties: Credit for theory versus experiment is unsettled.
The field may be too recent.
Practical advantage is not yet shown.
